reasoning: The proposal's core question — do diverse LLM autograders make the SAME errors against human labels, and does error correlation undermine the validity gain that ensembling/voting assumes from independence — is directly and fully answered by "Nine Judges, Two Effective Votes: Correlated Errors Undermine LLM Evaluation Panels" (arXiv 2605.29800), which runs a 9-judge panel across 7 model families on human-annotated items, computes per-judge error vectors, quantifies shared vs idiosyncratic error (the panel yields only ~2 effective independent votes; ~3/4 of nominal independence is lost), and concludes scaling panels cannot substitute for genuine independence — exactly the proposal's intended conclusion. This rests on the problem-level finding from "Correlated Errors in Large Language Models" (arXiv 2506.07962, ICML 2025) and "Great Models Think Alike and this Undermines AI Oversight" (arXiv 2502.04313), while "LLM Judges Inconsistently Disagree Across Safety Criteria and Harm Categories" (arXiv 2605.31381) covers the safety/refusal/harmfulness slice the proposal targets. The only differences are a specific dataset choice and specific open-weight judge models, which do not constitute a novel contribution; the methodology and findings are already published.

evidence.title: Nine Judges, Two Effective Votes: Correlated Errors Undermine LLM Evaluation Panels
evidence.summary: Runs a 9-judge panel across 7 model families on human-annotated NLI items, computes error correlation, and shows the panel provides only ~2 effective independent votes because judges make the same mistakes on the same items; actual panel accuracy falls 8-22pp short of what independent voting would achieve. Directly answers the proposal's question that ensembling does not improve validity the way independence would imply.

evidence.title: Correlated Errors in Large Language Models (ICML 2025)
evidence.summary: Establishes the problem-level finding that LLMs agree on wrong answers far more than chance, with correlation higher among same-developer/same-architecture models, and discusses direct implications for the LLM-as-judge paradigm — i.e., shared rather than idiosyncratic errors.

evidence.title: Great Models Think Alike and this Undermines AI Oversight
evidence.summary: Safety-framed analysis showing model errors are increasingly correlated as capability rises, undermining the independence assumption behind using one model to oversee/judge another — the core premise the proposal seeks to test.

evidence.title: LLM Judges Inconsistently Disagree Across Safety Criteria and Harm Categories
evidence.summary: Measures cross-judge agreement and disagreement specifically on safety/refusal/harmfulness criteria with human annotations, covering the exact safety-eval slice the proposal targets, including human-LLM alignment (Cohen's kappa ~0.64) and cross-judge consistency.

evidence.title: HarmMetric Eval: Benchmarking Metrics and Judges for LLM Harmfulness Assessment
evidence.summary: Benchmarks multiple judges/metrics for harmfulness assessment against reference labels, demonstrating that comparing judge error profiles on safety/harmfulness eval sets is an established, published practice.
